brief.head: Just do stuff
brief.text: Amit Varma learns by plunging in and working out first principles later. His gyan, he said, comes from bumbling through: “Just do stuff and you’ll learn from it.” {072-C14}

brief.head: Hearing a drought
brief.text: Bernie Krause recorded one Californian spot from 2004 to 2015. Eyes missed the species lost in a drought; “the soundscape captured everything”, Varma said. {072-S02}

brief.head: Thinking on paper
brief.text: Adam Smith could not have had his thoughts before books, Varma argued. Writing let him build layers of thought upon earlier layers, making him a better thinker. {072-C07}

brief.head: A voice in your head
brief.text: Radio must please five people in a car, Varma said, so it stays broad. A podcast is a voice in your head, intimate enough to go deep. {072-C09}

brief.head: One format at a time
brief.text: Ajay Shah learnt to write papers, then op-eds, then blog posts, then books, spending a couple of years inside each. Now all of them are “stored in my skull”. {072-S13}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the forms that shape art
lead.head: Thinking outside the vinyl
body: Why does a pop song last three minutes, an album forty and a feature film ninety? Not because audiences preferred them, Amit Varma argued in this week’s episode. Each form grew out of a constraint, and most of those constraints are gone.
Ajay Shah offered a line from Winston Churchill: “We make our buildings and then our buildings make us.”
Varma has his own version. “I say form shapes content, and content shapes character,” he said. {072-C01}

He learnt it from his own podcast, *The Seen and the Unseen*. A five-minute show can be shallow; a ten-hour one demands that you read all the guest’s books and listen without interrupting, and that, he said, makes you a different kind of person.
## Born of constraint
The rule runs through nature. Rainforest birds repeat calls in a narrow band so that something gets through; birds near the forest floor call low.
Music, too, takes the shape of its room, Varma said, following David Byrne. Out in the open, rhythm carries, so outdoor music is percussive.
In gothic cathedrals, where a note hangs in the air for more than four seconds, music grew slow and harmonically simple. In crowded, cluttered clubs it could be complex. Arenas favour metal.
Storage did the rest. The 78 RPM record held three minutes, hence the three-minute pop song. Columbia’s LP, which Varma dated to 1948, held about twenty minutes a side, hence the forty-minute album.
To those nostalgic for the concept album, his reply: “Dude, the concept album came about because there was a constraint in the storage.” {072-C05}
The conventions outlived the limits. Shah saw “powerful conformist forces” at work; Varma, a selection effect, since an eight-minute song got no radio play unless you were already Pink Floyd.
## Pages and screens
Writing followed the same path. Books settled between 100 and 300 pages, op-eds at 800 words. Blogging in the early 2000s freed Varma from both: he could write 80 words or 8,000.
On screen, a 90-minute feature film is a short story, he argued, and a streaming series is a novel. {072-C08}
As for short attention spans, he pointed out that people now binge eight hours of a series at a stretch.
## A golden age

The final part of the episode turned to money. Creators now own the means of production, Varma said, face no gatekeepers and no constraint of form, and can reach and earn from their audiences directly. {072-C10}
That frees them from the old need to scale, when only the very top artists earned a living. A thousand true fans paying $100 a year, in Kevin Kelly’s sum, is enough.
Shah asked whether this was survivor bias. Varma said no: more than a lakh Indian creators earn between one and ten lakh rupees a month.
He went further. With more people alive, more leisure and cheap tools, he argued, there should be more active creators today than in all earlier history combined.
Shah had a worry, half in jest: “Owing to the shortage of followers, the production of leaders has been discontinued.” {072-J11}
Varma objected that not everyone is a creator. Shah did the sums: about ten to the eighth potential followers and ten to the fifth creators, “so there’s still like an average of thousand each”.

second.label: The limits of print
second.head: Too big to bind
second.deck: Robert Caro wrote a million words; the printers could bind only 800,000
body: Amit Varma counts *The Power Broker*, Robert Caro’s biography of Robert Moses, among his favourite books. {072-R11} Caro delivered it to his publisher, Robert Gottlieb, at one million words.

Gottlieb asked his printers what they could do. The most they could bind, they said, without the book falling apart was 800,000 words. So a 200,000-word section on Jane Jacobs, “a hero to both you and me”, as Varma told Ajay Shah, was simply cut. {072-S10}

Today, Varma said, such a section would be uploaded or published as a book of its own. Then it was lost to history. Every printed book, he added, has a floor and a ceiling: most run between 100 and 300 pages.

quote.text: But at that time it’s just gone. It’s just lost to history.

second.caption: the 200,000 words that were cut

third.head: Solos born of majboori
body: Jazz sounds the way it does because of where it began, Amit Varma said. Early jazz was played in venues without amplification, so the loudest instruments won. {072-S06}
That is why the trumpet became popular, and why the banjo was preferred to the acoustic guitar. The guitar came back only when amplification arrived.

Improvisation had a practical start too. The early bands played for dancers, and when the written music ran out, the dancers still wanted to dance. {#dancers} “They’re paying customers, you gotta do what you gotta do,” Varma said. So the band stretched out with solos.
“So it was almost as coming out of majboori,” he said. “Today if they don’t improvise, we’ll demand our money back.”
third.caption: how jazz got its solos

p2.title: The tyranny of form
p2.deck: Songs, books and films were shaped by constraints that no longer apply, Amit Varma argued, chapter by chapter

sections.label: Understand form
sections.head: Listen to understand
sections.caption: long conversations and listening
body: When Amit Varma started *The Seen and the Unseen*, he assumed that people have short attention spans, that you must hook them early, and that an episode cannot run past 10 or 15 minutes. All of it, he said, was wrong.

The show grew from single-subject episodes of 15 or 20 minutes into three-hour deep dives, then into oral histories of eight hours and more. A recent one ran ten and a half hours. Ajay Shah said he was still waiting for his gold medal. Until the podcast ends, Varma replied, he is “the provisional gold”. {072-J02}

In an essay, *A Meditation on Form*, he worked out that this was not the same thing made longer. {072-R02} A five-minute show can be shallow. A seven- or eight-hour one demands all the guest’s books, knowledge of their field and a sense of their life. {072-S01}
## Listening without ego
It demands listening. “The key value that I learned from doing those long episodes is that you simply never interrupt,” Varma said.
He invoked Stephen Covey: we listen to respond, we don’t listen to understand. In a long conversation, he said, you have to listen to understand, with no room for ego. {072-J13}
That listening produces deeper, more relaxed content, and that, he said, changes the person doing it. {072-C01}
~ It works the other way too. Some content suits only one form: rapid-fire questions need five minutes, depth needs hours.

quote.text: The key to having a successful deep episode is that you allow the person to sink into their thoughts.

sections.label: The sound of rooms
sections.head: Rooms that wrote the music
sections.caption: how venues and storage shaped music
body: Amit Varma would pick one place and time to visit: CBGB’s in New York in 1975, where American punk and alternative rock were born. The club was crowded, cluttered and noisy. “And this was a feature, not a bug,” he said, because the mess absorbed sound and killed reverberation, making room for harmonically complex music. {072-S03}

The same logic defends AC/DC’s Angus Young, mocked for one kind of sound and three or four chords. In vast arenas you need a wall of sound, Varma recalled a guitarist telling Rick Beato, and for that Young’s style is perfect. {072-S04}
There is no hierarchy here, Varma said: Western classical music is not more evolved than drumming. {072-C04}
The Beatles left the stage, Ajay Shah noted, partly because the amplification of the day could not beat screaming fans, and they were heading to *A Day in the Life*.
## Thirty-second songs

New platforms bring new rules. Spotify pays once a track has played 30 seconds, so Vulfpeck released *Sleepify*, an album of 30-second songs for fans to loop as they slept. {#sleepify} The band made a fair bit of money until Spotify caught on.
~ TikTok counts a liked video as liked audio, so musicians are now told to be as indulgent as they like, as long as they deliver: “Give me that fifteen second hook I can put on TikTok.” {072-S09}

quote.text: There’s no hierarchy, there’s no value judgment. Particular kinds of music sound the way they do because of circumstances.

sections.label: The written word
sections.head: Eighty words or eight thousand
sections.caption: breaking free of the 800-word op-ed
body: Before the printing press, Amit Varma said, writing was limited by memory and by cumbersome scrolls. He showed *Der Edelstein*, an early printed book by Ulrich Boner. {072-R10}
Print then fixed the forms. Books settled between 100 and 300 pages; op-eds at 700 or 800 words, a thousand at most.
As a young would-be writer in the 1990s, Varma saw only two options: 800-word op-eds for the *Times of India* or the *Indian Express*, or a book of around 200 pages.
## Blogging’s release
Blogging in the early 2000s was a release. “I was not bound by form. I could write something in eighty words, I could write something in eight thousand words,” he said. {072-S12}
Nor was he bound by the news cycle or a gatekeeper. He averaged five posts a day for five years, about 8,000 posts, many just a line and a link. {#posts}
Social media later split blogging apart, he said: micro-blogging went to Twitter, personal posts to Facebook and Instagram. Newsletters revived it, letting a writer keep readers for life.
~ Ajay Shah learnt papers, op-eds, blogs and books one at a time, and now switches between them at will. {072-S13} With great modesty, Varma said, he had left out his latest form: YouTube.

quote.text: The fact that he can have the thoughts he did is that by writing, he is actually making himself a better thinker.

sections.label: Screens and voices
sections.head: Films are short stories
sections.caption: the feature film as a short story
body: When Amit Varma wanted to be a filmmaker, the forms on offer were the 90-minute Hollywood film, the three-hour Bollywood film and the half-hour TV show: 24 minutes of content and two three-minute ad breaks. {#doordarshan}
A 90-minute feature, he argued, is a short story, not a novel: one dominant narrative arc, one tension. {072-C08}

Streaming changed that. His favourite show, *The Wire*, made no attempt to hook the viewer, used no music beyond what played in the scene, and let fifteen or sixteen major characters unfold over seasons. {#wire}
What a 300-page book can do, he said, can now be done on screen.
## Closer and closer

Distance matters too. In a cinema, the screen is far from the viewer and the camera roughly as far from the actor, which suits westerns and car chases. {#cinema} Television sits a couple of metres away, which suits *Friends* and *Seinfeld*. A YouTube video is in your hand, all close-ups.
A ten-hour conversation, he added, is not ten one-hour ones: the rhythm is different.
~ His almost ten-hour episode with Rajeshwari Sengupta, *The Life and Times of the Indian Economy*, has passed 50,000 views on YouTube, though it is a thumbnail and two people talking. {072-S14}

quote.text: Actually a feature film of ninety minutes is equal to a short story. It’s not a novel.

sections.label: The golden age
sections.head: A thousand fans, no gatekeeper
sections.caption: the five changes for creators
body: Ajay Shah set up the question with a line from Stewart Brand: “We are as gods and we might as well learn to live like that.” Any teenager in her bedroom, he said, can now make a ten-hour video. How, he asked, does one find an audience?
Amit Varma listed five changes. Creators have the means of production, face no gatekeepers, are free of form, reach audiences directly and earn from them directly. {072-C10}

The old model was clumsy. A newspaper gathered readers’ eyeballs, sold them to advertisers and passed the writer a sliver, because micropayments had too much friction. And your attention is not free, Varma said: time is money.
## No need to scale

Once, only the very top artists earned anything; the mediocre artist starved in an attic. Kevin Kelly’s answer, in 2009, was a thousand true fans paying $100 a year. {072-R19} Li Jin’s was a hundred paying $1,000.
Bari Weiss, “a fellow winner of the Bastiat Prize”, started *The Free Press* on Substack; Varma had read that it is now valued at $100 million. {#weiss}
Is this survivor bias? No, Varma told Shah: more than a lakh Indian creators earn between one and ten lakh rupees a month. {#lakh}
~ Miss Excel, who teaches Excel while dancing on Instagram, became a star. “Any gatekeeper would laugh her out of the room,” Varma said. {072-S15}

quote.text: Kelly’s point is you don’t need to scale anymore.

side.boxText: Amit Varma calls David Byrne’s *How Music Works* a masterpiece, and gives it to everyone he meets. The book shows how rooms and technology, from gothic cathedrals to CBGB’s, shaped the music made in them. {072-R04}

contQuote.text: My sense is that we are living a golden age of all kinds of creative arts. We should have Beethovens and Bachs and Kumar Gandharvas all around us. We should have a Shakespeare in every nukkad.

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: A poetry newsletter, a symphony on a disc, and a star at the airport

stories.caption: Delhi’s poetry newsletters
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on poetry, print and Delhi before 1857
stories.head: Verse that sold the newspapers
body: Between about 1801 and 1857, Delhi was a city in transition. Amit Varma, drawing on Swapna Liddle’s *The Broken Script*, one of his favourite history books, described what happened when newspapers and newsletters took off. {072-R14}

For some reason Varma could not explain, poetry was hugely popular. “Newspapers would publish shayari because people would buy newspapers to read them,” he said. The emperor Zafar’s verses appeared, but so did other poets’. {072-S11}
Ajay Shah was struck by something else: “Unimaginable that an emperor would compose poetry.”

Then there were the mushairas, where poets gathered to recite to one another. One entrepreneur, much criticised in his time for his commercial instincts, decided that this had to be preserved. He was enjoying it so much, he reasoned, that others would love it too.
So he began publishing newsletters of all the poems recited at a mushaira, with an essay on matters of form at the start.
Varma saw forms stacked on forms: a mushaira in a physical space, a newsletter made possible by the printing press, and out of the two, a new form of learning.

Before that, Varma said, a student learnt poetry piecemeal: one person recited a poem, then another. Now there were critical essays and collections. Readers were exposed to “a large LLM, as it were”, and learnt much faster. {072-J08}
~ “It’s miraculous,” he said. It was almost like what the internet did for his own generation.
stories.why: A new medium laid over an old one can change how fast people learn. Varma set the mushaira newsletter beside the internet: each turned a scattered, chance encounter with an art into a fast, systematic education.
stories.postscript: Lest gossip seem modern: Rahul Matthan told Varma, in another episode, that 19th-century English newspapers were full of smut.

stories.caption: the length of a CD
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the arbitrary origins of a standard
stories.head: The disc that Beethoven measured
body: When Philips and Sony came together to invent the compact disc, Sony’s president was shown a disc by Philips that held sixty minutes and could go higher. He asked for seventy-four. {#cdsixty}
Why seventy-four? Amit Varma put the question to Ajay Shah, who got it at once: “The ninth of Beethoven?”
“Yeah, he was a big fan of Ludwig van Beethoven and Beethoven’s ninth symphony is seventy four minutes,” Varma said. {072-S07}

~ So for that arbitrary reason, a CD held 74 minutes of music; later CDs could hold more. The point, for Varma, was how such limits become conventions. There is no logical reason left to think in forty-minute albums, he said, but bands still do.
stories.why: Standards that feel natural often have arbitrary origins: the capacity of a whole medium was set by one executive’s favourite symphony. Listeners who mourn the concept album, Varma argued, are mourning a storage constraint. {072-C05}

stories.start: But when we look back at the ear earlier transitions
stories.end: it sort of fit conveniently into that world of FM radio
stories.caption: Dark Side of the Moon on FM radio
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on Pink Floyd and the one-hour block
stories.head: One album, one hour of FM
body: Looking back at the shifts from the 78 RPM record to the 33 RPM to the CD, Ajay Shah was struck by how few musicians ever broke with convention. {072-C06}

There were exceptions. Pink Floyd’s *Echoes*, he thought, takes up the whole of side two of *Meddle*. But mostly, he guessed, “there are powerful conformist forces that want you to fit into a mainstream world.”

Then there was *Dark Side of the Moon*. He had read that in the early years of FM radio, the album was a perfect match for the medium. Stations could play some ads, play the entire album, play some more ads, and that made a one-hour block. {072-S08}
~ Amit Varma added a selection effect. Unless you were already a superstar like Pink Floyd, an eight-minute song simply did not get played on radio.

quote.text: Play the entire Dark Side of the Moon, and then you play some ads, and that’s a one hour block.

stories.start: I'll often meet creators who are remarkably successful in what they do
stories.end: allowing them to be true to themselves and get beyond the tyranny of form
stories.caption: being stopped at airports
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on fame in the age of the niche
stories.head: Famous in a crowd of one
body: It happens often, Amit Varma said. He is at an airport, and someone stops him to thank him for his work. {072-S16}
“Nobody around has a faintest clue who I am,” he said. “They’re all looking and going, who’s this guy? But for this person, I’m Shah Rukh Khan.”

Fame, in his telling, now lives in small circles of devotion. He named the Peter Cat Recording Company, loved by him and his crew Nomsita and Vaishnav: “never gonna be the Beatles in terms of scale”, but the Beatles to their fans. {072-J21}
~ Mainstream adulation, the kind in which people build temples to Amitabh Bachchan, may have had its day, he said. {#temples} The intimate kind, he expects, will become more and more common.
stories.why: Fame has not vanished; it has moved into niches. A creator unknown to the crowd can be a star to the one person who stops him, and that devotion, Varma argues, is what pays. {072-C12}
stories.postscript: Ajay Shah had his own moment: a CRPF man at airport security, faced with a backpack holding a tripod, asked, “YouTube karte ho?” {072-S17}

quiz.q: Why does a compact disc hold 74 minutes, according to the story Varma told?
quiz.a: Sony’s president was a Beethoven fan, and the Ninth Symphony runs seventy-four minutes.

quiz.q: Where does the three-minute pop song come from, in Varma’s telling?
quiz.a: The 78 RPM record, the main storage of its day, held three minutes.

quiz.q: Why did early jazz bands favour loud instruments like the trumpet and the banjo?
quiz.a: Early jazz venues had no amplification, so bands needed loud instruments to be heard.

quiz.q: Why did Robert Caro’s *The Power Broker* lose a 200,000-word section on Jane Jacobs?
quiz.a: Printers said 800,000 words was the most they could bind without it falling apart.

quiz.q: Why, in Varma’s view, is a podcast not simply radio on demand?
quiz.a: Radio must please five people in a car; a podcast is a voice in your head.

quiz.q: What arithmetic lies behind Kevin Kelly’s idea of a thousand true fans?
quiz.a: A thousand fans paying $100 a year each make $100,000 a year.
